rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about which modality, encoder, profile setting, or aggregation strategy performs best. The most critical uncertainty is the absolute performance level of the simplest possible baseline, which anchors all future comparisons. 2) What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single profile, PCA-2000) establishes the minimal-complexity RNA baseline. It isolates the contribution of the RNA modality with a standard, fast linear encoder and no aggregation or fusion complexity. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: As the simplest configuration in the search space, it provides a clean reference point. Every subsequent experiment—varying the RNA encoder (scvi, scgpt), adding multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), adding an image modality, or testing fusion strategies—can be directly compared against this baseline to isolate the marginal effect of each design choice. Starting here maximizes the information gained per experiment under a limited budget, because it simultaneously calibrates the performance floor and sets up the clearest comparison axes for the next several runs.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: We have only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA) yielding ~48.5% accuracy. We have zero information about whether the image modality carries useful signal for this task. The most critical unknown is whether image features are informative at all, since this determines whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing. 2) What this tests: config_010 (image-only, single-profile, ResNet-50) establishes a second modality anchor under the same single-profile setting as config_001, isolating the effect of modality (RNA vs. image) while keeping profile complexity constant. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: Before investing budget in the large multimodal design space (configs 016–051), we must know whether each modality individually contributes. If image-only performs comparably to or worse than RNA-only, multimodal fusion is unlikely to add much and we should focus on improving the RNA encoder or profile setting. If image-only is substantially stronger, multimodal fusion becomes a high-priority direction. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design axis (modality) under the limited budget.

With only two completed experiments, we know RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) yields ~48.5% accuracy while image (resnet50, singleprofile) is much weaker at ~20.8%. The dominant uncertainty is whether the RNA representation quality can be improved. Config_004 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) isolates exactly one variable from config_001: replacing the linear PCA encoder with a learned scVI VAE representation (both 200-dim), while holding profile setting, aggregation, and modality constant. If scvi_n200 substantially outperforms pca_n2000, it tells us nonlinear learned representations are critical and we should invest in richer encoders (e.g., scGPT) and multimodal fusion built on them. If it performs similarly, PCA is sufficient and we should pivot to testing multiprofile/aggregation or multimodal fusion. This single-variable comparison is the most informative use of the next budget slot given the sparse evidence.

Evidence: We have two RNA-encoder data points at singleprofile/rna_only—pca_n2000 (acc 0.485) and scvi_n200 (acc 0.520)—showing that encoder choice matters (~3.5 pp gap). Image-only (resnet50) is very weak (0.208), so the RNA branch is the primary performance driver. Uncertainty: We have no data on the third RNA encoder, scgpt (a pretrained single-cell foundation model), and it could be substantially better or worse than scvi_n200. Question tested: config_007 (scgpt, singleprofile, rna_only) is a clean single-variable swap from config_004, isolating the RNA-encoder effect with no confounds from profile setting, aggregation, or fusion. Why this is the best next experiment: Before investing budget in multiprofile, multimodal, or aggregation/fusion variants, we need to know which RNA encoder to anchor on. Completing the three-way encoder comparison (pca vs scvi vs scgpt) at the simplest setting gives the most information per experiment and prevents us from propagating a suboptimal encoder choice into all downstream multimodal/multiprofile trials.

Evidence: scvi_n200 is the clearly best RNA encoder (0.5203 acc vs 0.4849 for pca_n2000 and 0.4106 for scgpt), and image-only is very weak (0.2079), suggesting RNA is the dominant signal. Uncertainty: we have only tested singleprofile so far and do not know whether multiprofile with aggregation improves the best RNA encoder. This experiment (config_005: rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) directly tests whether multiprofile + simple aggregation helps over the singleprofile baseline (config_004), changing only the profile/aggregation dimension while keeping the best encoder fixed. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it isolates the profile-setting effect on the strongest model, avoids confounding with image or fusion choices, and establishes whether the added complexity of multiprofile is worthwhile before investing in multimodal or transformer-aggregation variants.

Evidence: config_005 (scVI n200, multi-profile, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc, a large +0.13 jump over the same encoder in single-profile (config_004, 0.520), establishing multi-profile + scVI as the strongest direction. However, we have only tested one aggregation method (avgpool) in the multi-profile setting. Question: config_006 isolates the effect of aggregation (transformer vs avgpool) while holding RNA encoder (scVI n200) and profile setting (multi) constant, giving a clean 1-variable comparison against config_005. Why this is the best next experiment: it directly exploits our strongest evidence to reduce uncertainty about whether a more expressive aggregation mechanism (transformer) can further improve the already-promising multi-profile scVI pipeline. The answer determines whether we should adopt transformer aggregation in all subsequent multimodal experiments, making it a high-leverage decision under a limited budget.

Evidence: Multiprofile with scvi_n200 jumps from 0.520 (single) to 0.650-0.653 (multi), a ~13-point gain, while aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) barely matters. The critical open question is whether this multiprofile boost is a general property of having multiple views or is specific to scvi_n200's learned latent space. Config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) directly tests this by holding the encoder fixed at pca_n2000 (known singleprofile = 0.485) and changing only the profile setting. If pca_n2000 also gains substantially, multiprofile is a broadly useful design axis and we should prioritize it in multimodal configs; if it does not, scvi_n200 is essential for multiprofile to work, narrowing the search. This is a clean single-variable comparison that reduces uncertainty about a key design decision before investing limited budget in more complex multimodal experiments.

Evidence: Our best result is config_006 (scvi_n200, multi-profile, transformer, RNA-only) at 0.653 acc, and image-only resnet50 (config_010) is very weak at 0.208. The critical open question is whether adding an image modality to the strong RNA pipeline helps or hurts. Question: config_032 (scvi_n200, multi-profile, resnet50, transformer, concat) differs from config_006 only by the addition of resnet50 with concat fusion, cleanly isolating the effect of multimodal fusion. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly tests whether multimodal fusion adds value over our best RNA-only baseline. If it improves on 0.653, we know to invest in stronger image encoders (ViT-L) and fusion strategies. If it does not, we learn that resnet50 is too weak to contribute and should pivot to testing ViT-L (config_013/014/015) before committing further budget to multimodal. This single experiment resolves the highest-uncertainty design decision (is multimodal worth pursuing?) with a minimal, interpretable change from our strongest configuration.

The current best result (config_032: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat; acc=0.688) shows a modest +0.035 gain over the best rna_only multiprofile config (0.653), and image-only resnet50 was very weak (0.208). The key uncertainty is whether the image modality's limited contribution is due to the weak resnet50 encoder or is a fundamental limitation of the image modality for this task. config_038 is identical to config_032 except it swaps resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l, providing a clean single-variable A/B comparison that isolates image encoder quality. If ViT-L substantially improves multimodal performance, it validates investing in the image modality and opens the ViT-L multimodal space; if it does not, it indicates the image modality is inherently limited here and future budget should focus on RNA-side improvements. This is the highest-information experiment because it resolves a major design axis (image encoder quality) that has zero prior evidence, and the answer will shape all subsequent multimodal decisions.

The current best configuration (config_038: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) achieves 0.721 acc / 0.681 F1, clearly outperforming RNA-only multiprofile (0.653) and multimodal with resnet50 (0.688). However, the fusion strategy (concat vs. weighted) has never been tested in the multimodal setting—all completed multimodal runs used concat. Config_039 is identical to config_038 except for fusion=weighted, making it a clean single-variable test of whether learned/weighted fusion can further improve over simple concatenation in the strongest configuration. This is the best next experiment because: (1) it exploits the strong evidence that the scvi_n200 + ViT-L + transformer + multiprofile stack is the most promising direction, (2) it isolates the effect of fusion, an important and completely untested design axis, (3) it is a minimal one-variable change from the current best, avoiding confounds, and (4) under a limited budget, testing whether a small architectural tweak can push past 0.721 is more informative than exploring weaker encoder choices (e.g., scgpt, which scored 0.411 in single-profile RNA) or redundant aggregation comparisons (transformer vs. avgpool showed only a 0.003 gap in RNA-only).
